metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against the Weighted Additive rule (WADD) by creating compensatory trials where the most valid cue points to one option, while the sum of the less valid cues points to the other. TTB, being a non-compensatory 'one-reason' decision heuristic, will consistently choose the option favored by the single most valid discriminating cue. In contrast, WADD integrates all cues and will often favor the option with multiple weaker cues, as their combined validity outweighs the single best cue. By measuring the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the TTB prediction, we can strongly discriminate between data generated by TTB (high proportion) and WADD (low proportion).

In this experimental design, trials where the sum of features differs between Option A and Option B are specifically constructed to pit the most valid cue against a combination of less valid cues. Take The Best (TTB) is non-compensatory and always chooses the option favored by the single highest-validity cue, which in these specific trials is always the option with the FEWER total positive features. Thus, TTB will score near 0 on choosing the option with the higher feature sum. Weighted Additive (WADD) integrates all features, and because the sum of the less valid cues' validities outweighs the most valid cue, WADD will typically choose the option with the HIGHER feature sum. This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with the higher unweighted sum of features on trials where the sums are unequal, providing a stark divergence between the theories.

This metric isolates the three dissociative trial pairs where Rank-WADD and WADD make opposite predictions. It computes the proportion of choices that align with the Rank-WADD prediction on these specific trials. Data simulated under Rank-WADD will yield a high proportion (close to 1, modulo noise), whereas data simulated under WADD will yield a low proportion (close to 0).

The critical trial pair pits [1, 0, 0, 0, 1] against [0, 1, 1, 0, 0]. The WADD model, using cardinal validities [0.98, 0.70, 0.68, 0.66, 0.50], assigns a higher value to the first option (0.98 + 0.50 = 1.48) over the second (0.70 + 0.68 = 1.38). In contrast, the Rank-WADD model assigns linear rank weights (5, 4, 3, 2, 1) and thus prefers the second option (4 + 3 = 7) over the first (5 + 1 = 6). By calculating the proportion of times the second option [0, 1, 1, 0, 0] is chosen over the first, we obtain a metric where WADD predicts a value < 0.5 and Rank-WADD predicts a value > 0.5. Averaging across 16 repetitions per subject stabilizes the metric and minimizes between-subject variance.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the prediction of the deterministic Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic. The experimental design is specifically constructed so that TTB and the compensatory Weighted Additive (WADD) rule make opposite predictions on 7 out of the 8 trial types. Therefore, data generated by the TTB model will yield a high value on this metric (close to 1, minus lapses), while data generated by the WADD model will yield a very low value, as the combined weight of lower-validity cues generally outweighs the single highest-validity cue.

In Probabilistic TTB, feature evaluation stops at the first discriminating cue. By design, in every trial of this experiment, Option A possesses a single cue that is strictly more valid than any cue Option B possesses. Consequently, TTB always evaluates Option A's advantage first, predicting virtually identical choice probabilities for Option A regardless of whether Option B has one lesser cue (1v1 trials) or two lesser cues (1v2 trials). WADD, in contrast, is compensatory and integrates all cues. Giving Option B a second, albeit less valid, cue substantially increases its weighted sum, thereby significantly reducing the probability that Option A is chosen. This metric calculates the within-subject difference in the proportion of times Option A is chosen between 1v1 trials and 1v2 trials. TTB predicts a difference near zero (bounded by 0.07 due to rare multiple evaluation errors), whereas WADD predicts a large positive difference.

This metric calculates the impact of lower-validity cues on choice probability specifically when the top cue is discriminating. Under the Dual-Process Strategy Mixture (TTB + WADD), when the top cue is discriminating, the TTB component locks onto it and always chooses the favored option, making the choice probability highly insensitive to lower cues. In contrast, under pure WADD, all cues are integrated compensatory, so varying the lower cues will still produce a large swing in the probability of choosing Option A. Thus, the difference in P(Choose A) between trials where lower cues favor A versus favor B (while the top cue favors A) will be substantially larger for WADD than for the Mixture model.

This metric calculates the overall proportion of Option B choices specifically on trials where Option B has a strong compensatory advantage (at least 2 more positive cues than Option A). In the pure Weighted Additive (WADD) model, the sheer number of lower-validity cues for Option B easily compensates for Option A's single best-cue advantage, leading to a high probability of choosing B. In contrast, the Dual-Process Mixture model includes a Take-The-Best (TTB) component that is completely blind to compensatory cues and consistently chooses Option A across all these trials. Consequently, the Mixture model imposes a rigid 'glass ceiling' on the probability of choosing Option B (capped by the compensatory mixture proportion), leading to a significantly lower metric value than pure WADD.
